Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I have to be on guard all the time
The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'being followed or tracked' suggests an interpersonal/persecutory trauma context that is not supported by the other selected items and is hard to reconcile with the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by interpersonal assault-style vigilance to sounds and sudden movements, which does not fit well with the stated trauma of toxic chemical exposure unless there is additional unreported violent context.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies mistrust of others in a deceptive or persecutory sense; paired with 'being followed' it shifts the formulation toward interpersonal threat rather than contamination/exposure-related PTSD.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'Avoid authority figures' is difficult to connect to the rest of the profile and to toxic chemical exposure specifically; no other items indicate authority-linked fear, blame, or trauma reminders involving uniforms/institutions.

vignette: When Elena Morales, a fifty-seven-year-old detective, first encountered the ruptured chemical tank during a warehouse raid, the dense vapor filled her lungs before she could secure her respirator. She stood trapped as the stinging air paralyzed her diaphragm, while uniformed supervisors hesitated, their radios crackling with contradictory orders instead of rescue. That institutional silence did not fade. Instead, the sudden inability to draw breath became the catalyst that pulled the incident’s fragmented pieces forward, leaving them disconnected and refusing to settle into a coherent narrative. Each time the physical sensation of shortness of breath arose in the weeks that followed, it immediately flooded her nervous system with a state of constant readiness, causing her muscles to lock and her eyes to constantly scan the precinct periphery for imminent threats. The tightness in her chest did not merely signal physical distress; she had come to believe that the people who were supposed to protect her had abandoned her to suffocate, cementing a conviction that she would never again trust her own environment or feel normal emotions. This conviction that she had to remain permanently on guard quickly rewired her daily state. She was certain that the system would fail her again, which found her body bracing before any unexpected sound occurred, turning ordinary footsteps into potential warnings. That relentless expectation of danger actively pulled the traumatic memories back into her present awareness, preventing them from receding into the past. What frightened her most was when the sharp tang of antiseptic or a colleague’s sweat drifted past her during a late shift, as the visceral immediacy of those present-tense memories compelled her to cover her face with her hands and mentally force herself to calculate case details until the sensation passed. Her belief that she had to be on guard at all times amplified her sensitivity to bodily odors, which in turn drove her to duck away from uniformed figures entirely to escape the memory of their abandonment. These protective maneuvers, however, actively prevented the memories from ever resolving. By redirecting her attention away from the suffocating air or physically blocking her own gaze, she consistently stopped the recall process before it could complete. This deliberate interruption did not heal the wound; it reinforced the appraisal that she was emotionally hollow and perpetually vulnerable to unseen threats. The recurrent sense that the event was still unfolding actively convinced her that her emotions were permanently severed and that the original responders had truly failed her. Because she avoided authority figures to escape the panic, she deprived herself of the very support structures that might have grounded her, ensuring that hypervigilance remained the only viable strategy. Over the following years, this cycle solidified into a rigid routine that cost her professional standing. During her shift at the metropolitan crime lab, the moment a cleaning crew sprayed antiseptic near her desk, the familiar breathlessness surged, pulling the warehouse’s vapor back into her immediate perception. Her expectation of danger kept her scanning for sounds, which triggered the fragmented recall, which cemented her fear of institutional failure. Now, divorced and isolated, Elena finds that this exhausting loop has fractured her professional confidence. The routine of face-hiding and authority avoidance has cost her the lead investigator position she once held, as supervisors interpret her evasion as a lack of teamwork. What brought her to the clinic was a recent raid where the same chemical odor returned with full force, leaving her unable to step outside her car. She is most afraid that the emotional numbness she expects to feel permanently will be her reality, though she secretly hopes that understanding the mechanics of this cycle might finally allow her to breathe without waiting for the air to vanish.
